question:
Patient note:
A 67-year-old right-handed man was brought to the internal medicine clinic by his spouse for progressive lower-extremity swelling and increasing exertional dyspnea over the past four weeks. He reports that during this period he has had to elevate his legs at night to keep the swelling down and sleeps on two pillows because lying flat leaves him short of breath; despite these changes he still awakens once or twice nightly feeling "waterlogged." He recalls being told eight years earlier that an echocardiogram showed weakening of the pumping function of his heart after an episode of viral myocarditis, and he has intermittently taken loop diuretics and an ACE inhibitor since then, though his adherence has been inconsistent. He has never experienced crushing substernal chest pain, nor has he undergone coronary angiography, and he specifically denies any previous heart attack, episodes of sudden diaphoresis with jaw or arm pain, or need for cardiac stenting or bypass. He likewise denies leg claudication, nonhealing foot ulcers, or prior vascular surgery, and states he has never been told he has blocked arteries in his legs. When questioned about neurologic events, he reports no sudden unilateral weakness, facial droop, slurred speech, or loss of vision, and there is no recollection of hospitalizations for stroke. His spouse confirms that his memory remains sharp; he manages the household finances and assists grandchildren with computer homework without difficulty, and she has noticed no personality change, disorientation, or repetitive questioning. He has never carried an inhaler, has never been hospitalized for bronchitis or emphysema, and is able to walk a city block without wheezing, though the ankle edema slows him now. His past gastrointestinal history is notable only for occasional dyspepsia relieved by over-the-counter antacids; he explicitly denies episodes of hematemesis, melena, or prior endoscopic documentation of ulcers. Of greater significance, he was diagnosed five years ago with biopsy-proven hepatitis C–related cirrhosis. He has esophageal varices seen on surveillance endoscopy and mild splenomegaly on abdominal ultrasound; his most recent laboratory studies from six months ago showed a total bilirubin of 3.1 mg/dL, INR 1.7, and albumin 2.8 g/dL. He has never developed overt hepatic encephalopathy or ascites requiring paracentesis, but he does note easy bruising and sporadic epistaxis. Despite this chronic liver condition, he has never been found to have any solid tumors and has no family history of gastrointestinal or hepatic malignancy; routine age-appropriate colonoscopy two years ago was unremarkable. He has never received chemotherapy, radiation, or bone marrow-suppressive agents and has not been told of any abnormal white blood cell proliferation; complete blood counts in prior records show no evidence of leukocytosis or lymphadenopathy, and he has not experienced night sweats, drenching fevers, or unexplained weight loss. He has maintained normal fasting and postprandial glucose values on annual screening, and lifestyle counseling alone—primarily focusing on portion control and walking after meals—has sufficed to keep his hemoglobin A1c below 6%; he takes no oral hypoglycemics or insulin. Renal function has historically been normal with a baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL, and urine microalbumin checks have been negative. Physical examination today finds an alert, oriented gentleman in no acute distress, speaking full sentences. Blood pressure is 124/72 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Jugular venous distention is present at 9 cm H₂O. The point of maximal impulse is laterally displaced; S1 and S2 are audible with a soft S3 gallop and no murmurs. Bibasilar crackles are absent; breath sounds are vesicular throughout. The abdomen is scaphoid with a palpable left-sided liver edge that is firm and non-tender; no fluid wave is noted. There is pitting edema to the mid-shins bilaterally, without erythema or tenderness, and distal pulses are symmetric and strong. Neurologic examination reveals intact cranial nerves, full strength in all extremities, and normal sensation; gait is steady. The patient walks unassisted to the exam table and recalls three objects at five minutes. Initial assessment is decompensation of previously known systolic dysfunction in the setting of advanced chronic liver disease, with no evidence of ischemic heart disease, peripheral vascular occlusive disease, cerebrovascular insult, chronic lung pathology, peptic ulceration, diabetes requiring pharmacotherapy, renal impairment, or malignancy.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index adds age points to weighted comorbidity points, counting only the highest applicable severity within each disease category.
- Age 67 (60–69 years) → 2.
- Congestive heart failure: known systolic dysfunction with orthopnea, jugular venous distention, and pitting edema → 1.
- Moderate-to-severe liver disease: hepatitis C cirrhosis with esophageal varices establishes portal hypertension → 3. Do not add a separate point for mild liver disease.
- No documented prior MI, peripheral or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic pulmonary disease, connective tissue disease, peptic ulcer, diabetes, hemiplegia, qualifying renal disease, malignancy, or AIDS → 0.
Total: 2 + 1 + 3 + 0 = 6.
Final answer: 6
